entry: Capital of Jiangxi, China, in the north-central part of the province between the Jiuling Mountains and [[Poyang Lake]]. In recent decades it has become a major railway hub in southern China. The name, meaning "southern flourishing," was given in 201 BC, when the [[Han dynasty]] made the city the seat of Yuzhang Commandery. After 763 it was the provincial center of Jiangxi. The Tengwang Pavilion, constructed in 653, is celebrated in a 675 poem by Wang Bo. On August 1, 1927, the Nanchang Uprising, led by pro-communist officers of the [[Kuomintang]] under Soviet direction, held the city. Since 1949 the government has called Nanchang "the place where the [[People's Liberation Army]] was born." The city is home to Nanchang University and appears among the top 100 cities worldwide by scientific research output, according to the Nature Index.

American politician and 52nd speaker of the [[United States House of Representatives]], serving 2007–2011 and 2019–2023. A member of the [[Democratic Party (United States)|Democratic Party]], she was the first woman to lead a major party in either chamber of Congress and the first woman to hold the speakership. Pelosi has represented California's 11th congressional district, which includes most of [[San Francisco]], since 1987. During her second speakership the House impeached President [[Donald Trump]] twice, and the Senate acquitted him both times. In November 2025 she announced she would not seek reelection in 2026.

Mountain in the western [[Himalayas]], the ninth-highest on Earth, with its summit at 8,126 m (26,660 ft) above sea level. It lies just south of the [[Indus River]] in Gilgit-Baltistan, Pakistan-administered [[Kashmir]], and is the westernmost of the 14 eight-thousanders. The name derives from [[Sanskrit]] *nagna* ("naked") and *parvata* ("mountain"). Nicknamed Killer Mountain for its many climber fatalities, it is cited by Guinness World Records as the fastest growing mountain in the world, rising 7 mm (0.27 in) per year.

Capital of [[Jiangsu]] province, China, in the Yangtze River Delta. The name, meaning "Southern Capital," was formally applied in 1368, the first year of the [[Ming dynasty]]. The city served as capital of many Chinese dynasties, kingdoms and republican governments from the 3rd century to 1949, including the Eastern Wu, the Southern Tang and the Ming, and it is one of China's Four Great Ancient Capitals. It was the seat of the central government of the [[Republic of China (1912–1949)|Republic of China]] under the [[Kuomintang]] in 1927–1937 and 1946–1949, until the government relocated to [[Taipei]] at the end of the [[Chinese Civil War]]. The [[Nanjing Massacre]] took place here in 1937–1938. Nanjing became capital of Jiangsu in 1952. Its landmarks include the Presidential Palace, the Sun Yat-sen Mausoleum and the Ming Xiaoling Mausoleum.

Mass murder and rape of Chinese civilians and prisoners of war by the Imperial Japanese Army in [[Nanjing]], the capital of the Republic of China, from December 1937 to March 1938. It followed the Battle of Nanjing and the retreat of Chinese forces during the [[Second Sino-Japanese War]]. After Japanese troops entered the city on December 13, 1937, they executed captured soldiers and male civilians, raped women and girls, and destroyed a third of the city by arson. The International Military Tribunal for the Far East estimated more than 200,000 deaths, while newer estimates range from 100,000 to 200,000. An International Committee of Westerners created a Nanking Safety Zone that is credited with saving at least 200,000 lives. After the war, General Iwane Matsui and other commanders were found guilty of war crimes and executed. Some Japanese nationalists and historical revisionists have denied or minimized the massacre.

Capital of the Guangxi Zhuang Autonomous Region in southern China, known as the "Green City" for its lush subtropical foliage. It lies in a hilly basin with a [[Monsoon|monsoon]]-influenced [[Humid subtropical climate|humid subtropical climate]]. The area was part of Baiyue territory, and Jinxing County was established there in AD 318 under the [[Jin dynasty (266–420)|Eastern Jin]]. The city was renamed Yong prefecture in 632 during the [[Tang dynasty]] and Nanning, meaning "Pacified South," in 1318 under the [[Yuan dynasty]]. The Communist Party captured it on December 4, 1949. Nanning is the economic, financial and cultural center of Guangxi and the main training center for the Zhuang minority. It hosts the annual China–ASEAN Expo, begun in 2004, and serves as a gateway for cooperation with the [[ASEAN]] bloc.

Manipulation of matter with at least one dimension between 1 and 100 nanometers (nm). At this nanoscale, surface area and quantum mechanical effects become important in describing the properties of matter. The field overlaps with [[Organic chemistry|organic chemistry]], [[Molecular biology|molecular biology]], [[Semiconductor|semiconductor]] physics, energy storage and engineering. Its concepts were first discussed in 1959 by physicist [[Richard Feynman]] in his talk "There's Plenty of Room at the Bottom." K. Eric Drexler used the term in his 1986 book *Engines of Creation*, which proposed a nanoscale "assembler" able to build copies of itself. The scanning tunneling microscope, invented in 1981, allowed individual atoms to be imaged, and fullerenes were discovered in 1985. Applications include nanomedicine, nanoelectronics, energy production and consumer products. Concerns about the toxicity and environmental impact of nanomaterials have led to debate over special regulation.

City (pop., 2023: 327,734) on the [[Loire]] in western France, administrative seat of the Loire-Atlantique department and the Pays de la Loire region. Named after the Namnetes, a Gallic tribe, Nantes was a port on the Loire in classical antiquity and was captured by the Bretons in 851. It was the primary residence of the 15th-century dukes of [[Brittany]]. After the establishment of the [[French colonial empire]] in the 17th century, Nantes became France's largest port and was responsible for nearly half of the 18th-century French [[Atlantic slave trade]]. The French Revolution brought economic decline, and industries such as shipbuilding and food processing developed after 1850. Deindustrialization in the late 20th century led the city to adopt a service economy. Nantes received the European Green Capital Award in 2013, recognized for efforts to reduce air pollution and CO₂ emissions and for its public transport and biodiversity.

Ancient kingdom in southern China and [[Vietnam|northern Vietnam]], annexed by the [[Han dynasty]] in 111 BC. It was founded by the Chinese general Zhao Tuo, who had commanded Nanhai Commandery under the [[Qin dynasty]] and established the kingdom after the dynasty's collapse. Its territory covered the modern Guangdong, Guangxi, Hainan, [[Hong Kong]], [[Macau]] and southern Fujian regions. Its rulers called themselves emperor, though the Han court regarded Nanyue as a vassal state. In 113 BC Zhao Xing sought formal incorporation into the Han Empire, but his prime minister killed him. The next year [[Emperor Wu of Han]] sent 100,000 troops, who destroyed the kingdom. The state lasted 93 years under five generations of monarchs. Its rulers were of Han Chinese origin and introduced bureaucracy and writing to the region. Vietnamese historians have disagreed over whether Nanyue was a legitimate Vietnamese state, and its rulers are known there as the Triệu dynasty.

English model and actress, one of six models of her generation declared supermodels. She was the first Black woman to appear as a model on the covers of [[Time (magazine)|Time]] and [[Vogue (magazine)|Vogue]] France. Scouted in London in 1986, she walked for designers such as Gianni Versace and Azzedine Alaïa. Campbell has also released an R&B studio album, acted in film and television, and hosted the modeling competition *The Face* and its international versions. In 2024 she was banned from serving as a trustee of any U.K. charity for five years after a financial misconduct investigation.

Canadian author, social activist and filmmaker, born in [[Montreal]], known for criticism of corporate [[Globalization|globalization]] and capitalism. Her book *No Logo* (1999) brought her international attention. *The Shock Doctrine* (2007) analyzed the history of neoliberal economics, and *This Changes Everything: Capitalism vs. the Climate* (2014) was a *New York Times* nonfiction bestseller. In 2016 she received the Sydney Peace Prize for her climate justice activism. Since 2021 she has held a professorship in climate justice at the University of British Columbia, where she co-directs the Centre for Climate Justice.

Incendiary mixture of a gelling agent and a volatile petrochemical, usually gasoline or diesel fuel. The name is a portmanteau of the aluminum salts of naphthenic and palmitic acids that were its original thickeners. A team led by chemist Louis Fieser developed it in 1942 for the U.S. Chemical Warfare Service in a secret laboratory at [[Harvard University]]. Napalm burns at 800 to 1,200 °C (1,500 to 2,200 °F), longer than gasoline, and adheres to its targets. Its largest use was in airdropped incendiary bombs against Japanese cities in 1945, during [[World War II]]. The U.S. military also used it in the [[Korean War]] and the [[Vietnam War]], where over 388,000 tons were expended from 1963 to 1973. Napalm has fueled most flamethrowers used since World War II. The U.S. Armed Forces later used Mark 77 bombs as a successor to napalm.

Flammable liquid hydrocarbon mixture, generally a fraction of crude oil. It can also be produced from natural-gas condensates, petroleum distillates, and the distillation of coal tar and peat. In some industries and regions the name refers to crude oil or to refined products such as [[Kerosene]] or [[Diesel fuel|diesel fuel]]. Naphtha is used as a diluent and fuel and in the production of [[Plastic|plastics]]. It is known as Shellite in Australia. The word comes through [[Latin]] and [[Ancient Greek]] from Middle Persian *naft*, and in Ancient Greek it referred to any petroleum or pitch.

Organic compound (C₁₀H₈) consisting of two fused [[Benzene|benzene]] rings, a simple polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbon. It is a white crystalline solid with a characteristic odor detectable at concentrations as low as 0.08 ppm, and it is the main ingredient of traditional mothballs. Alexander Garden reported crystallizing it from coal tar in 1819. John Kidd proposed the name naphthalene, derived from [[Naphtha|naphtha]], in 1821. [[Michael Faraday]] determined its chemical formula in 1826, and Emil Erlenmeyer proposed its structure as two fused benzene rings in 1866.

City (pop., 2026: 905,050), capital of [[Campania]], southern Italy. Founded by Greek colonists, it is one of the oldest continuously inhabited urban areas in the world. It was the capital of the Kingdom of Naples and later of the Kingdom of the Two Sicilies until Italian unification in 1861. The city is considered a capital of the [[Baroque]], beginning with the work of [[Caravaggio]] in the 17th century, and it has been a global center of [[Opera|opera]] and classical music through the Neapolitan School. Its historic center is a [[World Heritage Site|UNESCO World Heritage Site]]. The University of Naples Federico II, founded in 1224, is regarded as the oldest state-funded secular university in the world. Neapolitan [[Pizza|pizza]]-making is on UNESCO's intangible heritage list. Naples is the third-largest urban economy in Italy by GDP, after Milan and Rome.

Emperor of the French (r. 1852–1870) and first president of the French Second Republic (1848–1852). Born Charles-Louis Napoléon Bonaparte, he was a nephew of [[Napoleon]] and the last monarch of France. He was elected president in 1848 and seized power by force in 1851, after he could not constitutionally be reelected. He founded the Second French Empire, which saw a rebuilding of Paris under prefect [[Georges-Eugène Haussmann]], expanded railways and modernized banking. He promoted construction of the [[Suez Canal]] and negotiated the 1860 Cobden–Chevalier Treaty with Britain. He allied France with Britain against Russia in the [[Crimean War]]. His support of Italian unification brought [[Nice]] and Savoy to France through the Treaty of [[Turin]]. The French intervention in Mexico failed. He was captured by [[Prussia]] at Sedan in 1870 during the [[Franco-Prussian War]], and the Third Republic was proclaimed. He went into exile in the United Kingdom.

French civil code established in 1804 during the French Consulate, and still in force in [[France]]. Officially the Civil Code of the French, it was drafted by a commission of four jurists, though [[Napoleon]] chaired many of its plenary sessions, and his support was crucial to its enactment. Its stress on clear, accessible law was a major milestone in abolishing the patchwork of feudal laws. Historian Robert Holtman regards it as one of the few documents to have influenced the whole world. It was the first modern legal code adopted with a pan-European scope, and it strongly influenced countries formed during and after the [[Napoleonic Wars]]. It also shaped legal reform in the [[Middle East]], while in [[Latin America]] Spain and Portugal had already established their own civil codes. Its categories derived from Justinian's [[Corpus Juris Civilis]].

Series of conflicts from 1803 to 1815 in which European coalitions fought France under [[Napoleon]]. Britain declared war on France in May 1803, and in 1805 Britain, Austria and Russia formed the Third Coalition. Napoleon defeated the Russo-Austrian armies at Austerlitz, which led to the dissolution of the [[Holy Roman Empire]]. He defeated Prussia at Jena-Auerstedt in 1806, and the [[Peninsular War]] drew British forces into Spain and Portugal. Napoleon's 1812 invasion of Russia ended in disaster for France. The Sixth Coalition defeated him at Leipzig in 1813, and coalition forces captured Paris in 1814. After escaping from Elba he ruled for about one hundred days before his defeat at Waterloo in June 1815, after which he was exiled to [[Saint Helena]]. The wars brought mass conscription and spread [[Nationalism|nationalism]] and [[Liberalism|liberalism]] across Europe. Britain emerged as the world's foremost naval and economic power.

Nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drug (NSAID) used to relieve pain, menstrual cramps and fever, and inflammatory diseases such as [[Rheumatoid arthritis|rheumatoid arthritis]] and [[Gout|gout]]. Sold as Aleve among other brands, it is also available over the counter. It works as a nonselective COX inhibitor that reduces prostaglandins. Its use carries an increased risk of heart disease, [[Stroke|stroke]] and gastrointestinal bleeding, and it is not recommended for people with [[Kidney|kidney]] problems. Naproxen was patented in 1967 and approved in the United States in 1976.

Peer-to-peer file-sharing application associated with the distribution of [[MP3]] files. Launched in June 1999 by Shawn Fanning and [[Sean Parker]], it was shut down in July 2001 after copyright lawsuits, including suits by [[Metallica]] and [[Dr. Dre]]. It filed for [[Bankruptcy|bankruptcy]] in June 2002. Roxio acquired its assets and relaunched it as a subscription service. Best Buy bought the service in 2008 for $121 million, and in 2026 it was relaunched as an [[Artificial intelligence|artificial intelligence]] tool.

Self-centered personality style marked by an excessive preoccupation with oneself and one's own needs, often at the expense of others. The term is named after [[Narcissus (mythology)|Narcissus]], the youth in Greek myth who fell in love with his reflection. Many psychologists regard a moderate degree of narcissism as normal and healthy, but extreme forms appear in [[Narcissistic personality disorder]]. Narcissism is also studied in the dark triad alongside subclinical [[Psychopathy|psychopathy]] and Machiavellianism. Narcissism began to be defined in psychological terms in the late 19th century, and [[Sigmund Freud]] published his theory of narcissism in 1914.

[[Personality disorder|Personality disorder]] characterized by grandiosity, entitlement, low [[Empathy|empathy]] and interpersonal difficulties. It may take a grandiose ("thick-skinned") form, marked by arrogance and exploitation, or a vulnerable ("thin-skinned") form, marked by shame and hypersensitivity to criticism. It is often comorbid with other mental disorders. The American Psychiatric Association's DSM gives two definitions, one categorical and one dimensional. There is no standard treatment, and [[Psychotherapy|psychotherapy]] is the main approach. Its causes are thought to be largely genetic and neurobiological.

Handsome youth in Greek mythology who falls in love with his own reflection in a pool of water. In the best-known version, found in [[Ovid]]'s *Metamorphoses*, Narcissus rejects many suitors, including the [[Nymph|nymph]] Echo. Under the influence of Nemesis he becomes infatuated with his reflection, remains by the pool until he dies, and a narcissus flower later grows there. An Oxyrhynchus papyrus from around 50 BC attests the myth. Narcissus was a popular subject in Roman art, appearing in nearly 50 Pompeian wall paintings. The figure gave his name to [[Narcissism]].

Genus of predominantly spring-flowering perennial plants in the amaryllis family, Amaryllidaceae. Common names include daffodil, narcissus and jonquil. The flowers have six petal-like tepals surmounted by a cup- or trumpet-shaped corona, and are generally white and yellow in the wild. The genus has about 70–80 species, and the Plants of the World Online database accepts 76 species and 93 named hybrids. The name may derive from Greek *narkō* ("to make numb") and is linked to the myth of [[Narcissus (mythology)|Narcissus]]. Native to southern Europe and North Africa, narcissi have been cultivated since ancient times, and thousands of [[Cultivar|cultivars]] exist. The plants produce [[Alkaloid|alkaloids]] that may be poisonous if ingested. Galantamine, produced from narcissi, is used to treat [[Alzheimer's disease|Alzheimer's dementia]].

Chronic neurological disorder that impairs the regulation of sleep–wake cycles, particularly REM sleep. Symptoms include excessive daytime sleepiness, [[Hallucination|sleep-related hallucinations]], [[Sleep paralysis]] and cataplexy, a sudden loss of muscle tone triggered by strong emotion. Type 1 narcolepsy features cataplexy and low orexin levels in the cerebrospinal fluid, while type 2 does not. Type 1 is thought to be an [[Autoimmune disease|autoimmune]] disorder, possibly triggered by an infection such as H1N1 influenza. There is no cure, but medications such as modafinil, sodium oxybate and [[Methylphenidate|methylphenidate]] can help. Untreated narcolepsy increases the risk of motor vehicle collisions and falls.
